header.title: Algorithms for Geometric Constructions
header.subtitle: Program a compass and straightedge to bisect and build exact angles

meta.lesson-focus: Design an algorithm using pseudocode or a flow chart to construct or bisect an angle with compass and straightedge; describe each step precisely; test for correctness on multiple cases; extend to algorithms for animated geometric constructions or visual proofs.
meta.ac9-descriptor-text: design, test and refine algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions based on geometric constructions and theorems; discuss and evaluate refinements
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Trigonometric ratios are an application of the property of similarity for right-angled triangles

html.section0_intro: Today you write step-by-step instructions that a machine could follow to construct exact angles. These three questions check the angle and flow-chart skills you will need.
html.section_warmup:
A real situation that is secretly today's maths.

A sign shop owns a laser engraver. It cannot use a protractor. It only knows two moves: draw an arc (like a compass) and draw a straight line through two points (like a ruler with no markings).

The shop is charged $2.50 for every instruction the engraver runs. A vague instruction such as “draw a line about halfway” wastes an acrylic sheet. A missing step wastes money too.

To cut an exact angle, the shop needs an algorithm: precise steps, in order, with decisions where needed. Today you design compass-and-straightedge algorithms that bisect an angle and construct 60°, 30° and 15°, then test and refine them so they work every time and cost less.

html.section3_desc: Drag each instruction into ✓ Precise enough for the engraver or ✕ Too vague. A precise step says exactly where the compass goes and what to draw.
html.sort_activity:
Could a machine follow this instruction exactly?
Place the compass point on O. Draw an arc somewhere near the angle. Keep the compass width the same as the last arc. Draw the line roughly in the middle. Mark A where the arc crosses arm OX. Set the compass to a sensible size. Draw a ray from O through P. Fix the angle if it looks wrong.

✓ Precise enough for the engraver

✕ Too vague

💡 Words like somewhere, roughly, sensible and looks wrong need human judgement. An algorithm names the exact point, the exact width and the exact line, so two people (or two machines) running it get the same result.
html.section4_heading: Match each construction to its angle
html.worked_example:
Design an algorithm that bisects any angle ∠AOB using only a compass and a straightedge, then test it on three angles: 80°, 150° and 30°.

1
Design the steps
Every step names the compass centre, the width and what to mark. The arcs from A and B use the same width, so P is the same distance from A as from B.
2
Write it as pseudocode, with a decision
If the width is too small, the arcs from A and B miss each other. The algorithm needs a decision to handle that.
1 PLACE compass on O; DRAW an arc crossing both arms
2 MARK A and B where the arc crosses the arms
3 SET width w greater than half of AB
4 DRAW an arc centre A, width w, inside the angle
5 DRAW an arc centre B, same width w
6 IF the arcs do not cross THEN increase w; GO TO 4
7 MARK P where the arcs cross
8 DRAW the ray OP; OUTPUT “OP bisects ∠AOB”
3
Test with three cases
Run the algorithm on an ordinary angle, a large (obtuse) angle and a small angle, then measure both halves.
80° → ∠AOP = 40°, ∠POB = 40° ✓
150° → ∠AOP = 75°, ∠POB = 75° ✓
30° → ∠AOP = 15°, ∠POB = 15° ✓
Why it works OA = OB (same arc) and AP = BP (same width), and OP is shared. So triangles OAP and OBP are congruent (SSS), and ∠AOP = ∠POB every time.
html.we_do_intro: Construct a 60° angle with no protractor, then turn it into 30°. An animator will also show the construction one frame per instruction. Work through it together.
html.strategy_section:
★Order the algorithm: a 30° angle

This algorithm combines the 60° construction with the bisector, but the steps are jumbled. Use ▲ and ▼ to put them in an order a machine could follow, then click Check order. Ask: does this step use a point that has not been marked yet?

Goal: construct ∠AOP = 30° using only a compass and a straightedge.
  • DRAW ray OB (∠AOB = 60°).
  • DRAW a ray from O; MARK A on it.
  • DRAW ray OP; OUTPUT ∠AOP = 30°.
  • PLACE compass on A, same width; MARK B where it crosses the first arc.
  • DRAW equal-width arcs centred on A and on B; MARK P where they cross.
  • PLACE compass on O, width OA; DRAW a long arc through A.

★Test and refine: spot the bug

Jordan wrote a bisector algorithm and tested it on a 70° angle. The test failed: the two angles came out as 19° and 51°. Click the line where Jordan's algorithm first goes wrong.

Test case: bisect ∠AOB = 70°. Expected output: two angles of 35°.
1 Compass on O, width 4 cm: draw an arc crossing both arms at A and B.
2 Compass on A, width 3 cm: draw an arc inside the angle.
3 Compass on B, width 5 cm: draw an arc crossing the first at P.
4 Draw the ray OP and output “OP bisects ∠AOB”.

✓ Right: that's the bug.

Why: P must be the same distance from A and from B. With widths of 3 cm and 5 cm, AP ≠ BP, so triangles OAP and OBP are not congruent and OP leans towards A. Refinement: write “keep the same width” into line 3, and test again on more than one angle.

Now fix line 3: what width, in cm, should the arc centred on B use?

retrieval.q: An angle of 84° is split into two equal parts. How many degrees is each part?
Each angle in an equilateral triangle is how many degrees?
In a flow chart, which shape holds a yes/no decision? Type the shape's name.
retrieval.hint: It is the shape with four equal sides standing on a corner.

fb.rectangle: A rectangle holds a process step. Decisions branch two ways from a different shape.

matchTerms.html: Arcs from O and A, same width

weDo.q:
1 DRAW ray from O; MARK A on it
2 DRAW arc centre O through A (width OA)
3 DRAW arc centre A, same width; MARK B where the arcs cross
4 DRAW ray OB; OUTPUT ∠AOB
The width is 5 cm, so OA = 5 cm. How long is AB, in cm?
weDo.hint: B is on the arc centred at A, drawn with the same 5 cm width.

fb.10: AB is one compass width, not two. B sits on the arc centred at A, so AB = 5 cm.

weDo.q: OB is also 5 cm (B is on the arc centred at O). Triangle OAB is equilateral. What is ∠AOB, in degrees?
weDo.hint: Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 180° ÷ 3.

fb.180: 180° is the angle sum. An equilateral triangle shares it equally between three angles.

weDo.q: Now run the bisector algorithm on ∠AOB. What size is each new angle, in degrees?
Animation. The 60° construction has 4 instructions and the bisector algorithm adds 4 more (3 arcs and 1 ray). How many frames does the full 30° animation need?

practice1.q:
Which instruction must come first in the bisector algorithm?
A) Draw the ray OP
B) Draw an arc centred on O crossing both arms
C) Draw an arc centred on A
Type A, B or C.
practice1.hint: A and B have to exist before you can put the compass on them.

fb.c: The compass cannot go on A until A has been marked. Which arc marks A?

practice1.q: How many arcs does the bisector algorithm draw?
practice1.hint: One from O, one from A, one from B.

practice1.q: Test case. The bisector is drawn on a 140° angle. The student measures ∠AOP = 70°. What should ∠POB measure, in degrees, if the algorithm worked?
practice1.hint: A bisector makes the two angles equal.

practice1.q: The 60° algorithm is run, then run again starting from ray OB to make ray OC. What size is ∠AOC, in degrees?
The arcs from A and B use the same width, 4 cm. P is where they cross. How long is BP, in cm?
practice1.hint: P is on the arc centred at B.

practice2.q:
1 SET angle = 60
2 REPEAT 3 times:
3   BISECT the angle; SET angle = angle ÷ 2
4 OUTPUT angle
What does this algorithm output, in degrees?

fb.20: Bisecting divides by 2 each time; it does not divide 60 by 3.

practice2.q:
1 SET angle = 90; SET count = 0
2 WHILE angle > 10:
3   BISECT; SET angle = angle ÷ 2; SET count = count + 1
4 OUTPUT count
What does this algorithm output?
practice2.hint: 90 → 45 → 22.5 → 11.25 → 5.625. Count the bisections until the angle is no longer above 10.

fb.3: After 3 bisections the angle is 11.25°, still greater than 10, so the loop runs once more.

practice2.q: In the bisector algorithm AB = 7 cm. The width for the arcs from A and B must be greater than half of AB. What is the smallest whole number of cm that works?
practice2.hint: Half of 7 is 3.5. The width must be more than that.

fb.3.5: At exactly 3.5 cm the arcs only touch on AB itself. The width must be greater than half of AB.

practice2.q: AB = 7 cm and a student uses a width of 3 cm for the arcs from A and B. Will the arcs cross? Type yes or no.
practice2.hint: 3 + 3 = 6, which is less than the 7 cm gap between A and B.

practice2.q:
Which algorithm produces a 15° angle?
A) Construct 60°, bisect once
B) Construct 60°, bisect twice
C) Bisect a right angle twice
D) Construct 60°, bisect four times
Type A, B, C or D.
Rays OB (at 60°) and OC (at 90°) are both measured from arm OA. The angle ∠BOC is bisected by ray OD. What size is ∠AOD, in degrees?
practice2.hint: ∠BOC = 30°. Half of it is 15°, added on to 60°.

fb.15: 15° is ∠BOD. The question asks for the angle from OA, so add ∠AOB = 60°.

practice3.q: The engraver charges $2.50 per instruction (each arc or line is one instruction). The bisector algorithm draws 3 arcs and 1 ray. What does one bisection cost, in dollars?
A 30° cut runs the 60° construction (2 lines and 2 arcs) and then the full bisector algorithm (3 arcs and 1 line). At $2.50 per instruction, what does the 30° cut cost, in dollars?

fb.10: That only counts one of the two algorithms. Add the 60° construction too.

practice3.q: Refinement. The arc from O in the 60° construction already crosses both rays, so it marks A and B for the bisector. The refined algorithm skips the bisector's arc from O. What does the 30° cut cost now, in dollars?

fb.20: That is the unrefined cost. The refinement removes one arc.

practice3.q: The shop takes an order for 40 signs, each with one 30° cut. How much does the refinement save on the whole order, in dollars?

fb.2.5: That is the saving on one sign. There are 40 signs.

Jordan's bisector algorithm says “draw an arc from A, then draw an arc from B” but does not say the widths must match. Explain why the arcs from A and B must use the same width.
exitProbs.hint: Think about what P must be the same distance from.
